cards.explanation: The answer is the herd or the flock, friends. The LORD tells Moses, Israel's leader, to say to the people: “…you may bring as your offering an animal from the herd or the flock.” (Leviticus 1:2) A bull comes from the herd, and a few verses later the flock turns out to mean sheep or goats (Leviticus 1:10). Two choices, both named, and nobody had to guess.

The answer is an unblemished male, friends. The LORD says, “If his offering is a burnt offering from the herd, he is to present an unblemished male.” (Leviticus 1:3) Two words do the work there: male and unblemished. God was specific, so the man brings what God asked for.

The answer is the entrance to the Tent of Meeting, friends. The man brings it “…to the entrance to the Tent of Meeting for its acceptance before the LORD.” (Leviticus 1:3) That's the same tent the LORD spoke from when He called to Moses, Israel's leader. The place is named, so there's no wandering around looking for it.

The answer is so it can make atonement for him, friends. The text says, “He is to lay his hand on the head of the burnt offering, so it can be accepted on his behalf to make atonement for him.” (Leviticus 1:4) The hand on the head is part of how the offering is accepted for him. The man isn't just a bystander at his own offering.

The answer is Aaron's sons the priests, friends. The text says, “…Aaron’s sons the priests are to present the blood and splatter it on all sides of the altar at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting.” (Leviticus 1:5) The man has his own jobs, like slaughtering the young bull before the LORD. Presenting and splattering the blood is the priests' work.

The answer is True, friends. The text says, “The entrails and legs must be washed with water, and the priest shall burn all of it on the altar…” (Leviticus 1:9) The word is must, so the washing comes first. Same instruction shows up again for the flock (Leviticus 1:13).

The answer is all of it, friends. First the animal is skinned and cut into pieces (Leviticus 1:6), and the entrails and legs are washed. Then the text says, “…the priest shall burn all of it on the altar as a burnt offering…” (Leviticus 1:9) Everything laid on that altar gets burned, with nothing held back.

The two answers are sheep and goats, friends. The text says a burnt offering from the flock means “…the sheep or goats…” (Leviticus 1:10), so either one works. The rule stays the same for both: he is to present an unblemished male.

The answer is the north side, friends. The text says, “He shall slaughter it on the north side of the altar before the LORD…” (Leviticus 1:11) Then the priests splatter the blood against the altar on all sides. The side of the altar is named right there in the verse.

The answer is a turtledove or a young pigeon, friends. The text says, “If, instead, one’s offering to the LORD is a burnt offering of birds, he is to present a turtledove or a young pigeon.” (Leviticus 1:14) So the burnt offering isn't only about bulls and sheep. Birds are on the menu too, and I love that the verse is so specific about which ones.

The answer is False, friends. The text says, “He shall tear it open by its wings, without dividing the bird completely.” (Leviticus 1:17) The head has already been twisted off (Leviticus 1:15) and the crop removed (Leviticus 1:16), so this bird isn't whole anymore. But it isn't split in two either. Then the priest burns it on the altar atop the burning wood.

The two answers are oil and frankincense, friends. The text says, “When anyone brings a grain offering to the LORD, his offering must consist of fine flour. He is to pour olive oil on it, put frankincense on it…” (Leviticus 2:1) The oil is poured on top, and the frankincense goes on it too. The priest later burns the handful together with all the frankincense (Leviticus 2:2).

The answer is that the rest belongs to Aaron and his sons, friends. The priest burns a handful as the memorial portion, and the remainder is theirs (Leviticus 2:3). They're the priests (Leviticus 1:5). The text calls it “…a most holy part of the food offerings to the LORD.” I would have guessed the man takes it home, so I'm glad the text is clearer than my guessing.

The answer is fine flour with oil, friends. Baked in an oven, it's fine flour with unleavened cakes mixed with oil or wafers coated with oil (Leviticus 2:4). On a griddle it's fine flour mixed with oil (Leviticus 2:5), and in a pan it's “…fine flour with oil.” (Leviticus 2:7) Different cookware, same two things.

The answer is True, friends. For the griddle offering, the text says, “Crumble it and pour oil on it; it is a grain offering.” (Leviticus 2:6) It's unleavened bread made of fine flour mixed with oil (Leviticus 2:5). So crumbling and pouring both happen.

The two answers are leaven and honey, friends. The verse says, “…you are not to burn any leaven or honey as a food offering to the LORD.” (Leviticus 2:11) That's why the oven versions are unleavened cakes and unleavened wafers (Leviticus 2:4). Bakers love a good rise, but leaven sits this one out, and even a guy who stamps cookies all day has to respect the honey rule too. Verse 12 adds that they must not go up on the altar as a pleasing aroma.

The answer is True, friends. The text says, “You may bring them to the LORD as an offering of firstfruits, but they must not go up on the altar as a pleasing aroma.” (Leviticus 2:12) So leaven and honey can still come to the LORD as firstfruits. The limit is that they must not go up on the altar as a pleasing aroma.

The answer is salt, friends. The text says, “And you shall season each of your grain offerings with salt.” (Leviticus 2:13) Then it adds, “you are to add salt to each of your offerings.” That's every offering, no exceptions.

The answer is crushed new grain roasted on the fire, friends. The LORD says, “If you bring a grain offering of firstfruits to the LORD, you shall offer crushed heads of new grain roasted on the fire.” (Leviticus 2:14) New grain, crushed, roasted on the fire. It's a different recipe from the flour ones.

The answer is True, friends, and both halves hold. The firstfruits grain gets oil and frankincense (Leviticus 2:15). Then the priest burns the memorial portion of the crushed grain and the oil, together with all its frankincense (Leviticus 2:16). Hold on to that pattern, because it shows up again in this passage.

The answer is a male or female without blemish, friends. The text says, “If one’s offering is a peace offering and he offers an animal from the herd, whether male or female, he must present it without blemish before the LORD.” (Leviticus 3:1) So either one works. The animal has to be without blemish.

The answer is True, friends. For the peace offering, the man lays his hand on its head and slaughters it at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting (Leviticus 3:2). The burnt offering started the same way, with a hand on the head (Leviticus 1:4). After that, Aaron's sons the priests splatter the blood on all sides of the altar.

The answer is the fat and kidneys and liver lobe, friends. The text lists “the fat that covers the entrails, all the fat that is on them, both kidneys with the fat on them near the loins, and the lobe of the liver…” (Leviticus 3:3-4) That's the food offering from the peace offering. Aaron's sons then burn it on the altar atop the burnt offering (Leviticus 3:5).

The answer is the entire fat tail, friends. For a lamb, the list includes “the entire fat tail cut off close to the backbone…” (Leviticus 3:9) It comes right before the fat that covers the entrails. Only the lamb has the tail on the list.

The answer is fat, friends. The text says, “Then the priest is to burn the food on the altar as a food offering, a pleasing aroma. All the fat is the LORD’s.” (Leviticus 3:16) Every time the list came up, fat was the first item. Now the LORD says all of it is His.

The two answers are fat and blood, friends. The LORD says, “You must not eat any fat or any blood.” (Leviticus 3:17) The fat is the same fat the LORD said belongs to Him in verse 16. Throughout the chapter, the priests splatter the blood on the altar, and the people are told not to eat it.

The answer is False, friends. The LORD says, “This is a permanent statute for the generations to come, wherever you live: You must not eat any fat or any blood.” (Leviticus 3:17) It's permanent, for the generations to come, and it applies wherever they live. So it doesn't stop at the tabernacle.
